Notes

贱

贱 is a harsh self-insult with meanings including “cheap” or “base.” Here the next lines explain the complaint: life is going well, yet the speaker is bored. “A sucker for punishment” conveys that self-reproach more naturally than calling him inexpensive.

  • Genius community transcript
盲流子

为艺术献身 is the elevated language of dedicating or sacrificing oneself to art. 盲流子 is a contemptuous label for a rootless drifter. Putting them into one description punctures the heroic artist image from inside: noble dedication and an unflattering social label refer to the same person.

  • Genius community transcript
上火

上火 can mean becoming angry or agitated, alongside its traditional bodily “heat” sense. Here it leads into a restless climate and nerves that will not relax. The word makes the emotional condition feel heated and physical without naming a particular illness.

  • Genius community transcript
  • Ministry of Education dictionary: 上火
背不完的锅

背锅, literally “carry the pot,” means take the blame, often for someone else. 背不完 makes it inexhaustible: however much blame he takes, there is more left to carry. The same image returns explicitly as 黑锅 in “Snatch.”

  • Genius community transcript
黄粱一梦

黄粱一梦 is the “yellow-millet dream” idiom: worldly glory proves brief and insubstantial, like a dream, or a desire comes to nothing. The following departure from the mortal world and repeated closing of the eyes turn that compressed literary phrase into a sequence of endings.

  • Ministry of Education dictionary: 黃粱一夢
撒手人寰

撒手人寰 is a literary euphemism for death: let go of the human world. Its solemn four-character form follows 黄粱一梦, then collapses into the short, repeated command to close the eyes. The sequence moves from polished literary language to a bare bodily action.

  • Genius community transcript
  • Ministry of Education dictionary: 撒手人寰
快乐

快乐 and 幸福 overlap, but the first emphasizes feeling happy or joyful; the second can describe a fulfilled, fortunate life. Using two different English questions preserves the widening scale before the everyday “How have you been?”

  • Genius community transcript
